source.title: MuLoCo: Muon is a practical inner optimizer for DiLoCo
source.authors: Benjamin Th'erien; Xiao-Long Huang; Aaron Defazio; Irina Rish; Eugene Belilovsky

record.file_problem: none; full paper text, including appendices, is supplied.
record.tranche_reason: Tests how batch size affects held-out evaluation loss in dense language-model pretraining, extending large-batch findings to MuLoCo and DiLoCo. It does not measure train–test gaps or test the other claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports batch-size effects on final evaluation loss in Section 7.2 and Figure 12. Other findings, including worker scaling and pseudogradient alignment, do not measure the behaviors named in the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study tests V5 in dense language-model pretraining by varying batch size at fixed model size and token budget, with hyperparameters retuned at each batch size. The 3.07B experiments use 61.4B training tokens, so larger batches receive fewer updates under the same data budget.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's batch-size paraphrase is accurate but narrow. The authors conclude that MuLoCo has larger critical batch sizes than DiLoCo at every tested worker count, improves worker scaling relative to the respective data-parallel baselines, and gives K=1 a favorable performance–training-time tradeoff. At 15B, its larger batches achieve comparable performance to smaller-batch baselines.
record.recipe_differences: Dense language-model pretraining with DiLoCo/MuLoCo and tuned batch sizes; evaluates final held-out loss rather than train–test generalization gap. The study also varies workers and synchronization intervals.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size and worker count change the reported evaluation-loss behavior.

fits_no_version.finding: Muon-based pseudogradients have stronger directional alignment, more stable step norms, and less spectral interference than AdamW-based pseudogradients.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inner-optimizer update structure affects pseudogradient quality during distributed training; these measures do not establish magnitude-aware sharpness or a train–test-gap relationship.

record.problems: The batch-size results are presented mainly as curves; text gives qualitative trends but not the batch-specific loss values. Hyperparameters are tuned separately for each batch size, so this does not isolate a fixed training recipe.
record.rows_left_out: Worker-scaling and pseudogradient-analysis results were excluded because they do not measure a behavior named by the versions. Figure 12’s exact batch-specific values are not recoverable from the supplied text.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization in the same architectures and training recipes.
Width increases beyond interpolation at convergence.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive methods versus SGD or momentum SGD under limited or broader tuning. Nesterov SGD is an outer optimizer here, not a standalone SGD comparator.

Image classifiers; longer-training remedies; isolated effects of warmup, learning-rate scaling, normalization, or regularization changes. Batch-size experiments retune several hyperparameters and do not isolate their individual contributions.
Dropout interventions and their dependence on dataset size or augmentation.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness, generalization gaps, and comparisons with norm- or margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized training examples versus random removal.

missing.what: DP Muon's batch-size response is omitted despite being a Figure 12 comparator. The text explicitly identifies its optimal batch size as 1M tokens and reports MuLoCo K=1 matching that optimal performance at 8M tokens per batch.

The 15B fixed-budget experiment reports comparable final loss and downstream performance for MuLoCo K=1 at 16.8M tokens per batch versus DP Muon at 4.2M and DiLoCo K=1 at approximately 1M. Record this as a comparison of adapted recipes, not an isolated batch-size intervention; hyperparameters were extrapolated without a 15B sweep.

record.verdict_notes: A train–test-gap measurement is unnecessary for V5, which names held-out performance under a fixed training budget. Exact Figure 12 losses cannot be reconstructed from the supplied text. The critical-batch-size inequality in Section 7.2 contains an apparent typo: Figure 1 defines the threshold as 1.01 times optimal loss, not 0.01 times optimal loss. Tables 3 and 7 also report inconsistent 15B loss values; retain the qualitative comparison without selecting an unexplained numerical value.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence; held-out performance with random labels.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation and test error as width increases.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and architectural bias.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum on image-classification or language benchmarks under the stated tuning conditions.
The study tunes hyperparameters separately at each batch size and does not report a direct train–test generalization gap. It tests dense language models, not image classifiers.
Dropout effects and interaction with data augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to the train–test gap.
Removing highly memorized examples and measuring the effect on test accuracy.
